_about: Links v2 of design 2026-11-15-onboarding-trust §6, with the derivations of §2.3 and the verdict strings and order of §2.4.

Hand-authored from the independent oracle in tools/vector-gen/oracle (Node WebCrypto and @noble; no andvari code). Regenerate with `npm run generate` there; `npm run check` fails on any difference. Secrets, nonces and envelope nonces are fixed.

derive: from the 32-byte link secret s. linkId = b64url(HKDF(s, "andvari/v2|link|id", 16)); offerKey and answerKey = HKDF(s, "andvari/v2|link|offer" / "andvari/v2|link|answer", 32), with ADs "andvari/v2|link-offer|" + linkId and "andvari/v2|link-answer|" + linkId; registerToken = b64url(HKDF(s, "andvari/v2|link|register", 32)); tokenHash = b64url(SHA-256 over the 43 ASCII characters of the token). HKDF-SHA-256, empty salt.
fingerprint: F = b64url(SHA-256(the creator's raw 32-byte identityPub)[0..16]), 22 characters.
commit / reveal: commit = hexLower(SHA-256("andvari/v2|code-commit|" + b64url(nonce))). A reveal that does not hash to the offer's commit is bad_reveal.

code: a link has TWO comparison codes, one per side (§2.3, §6.11). code(side) = u32be(SHA-256(inputUtf8)[0..4]) mod 10^6, zero-padded to 6 digits, with inputUtf8 = "andvari/v2|link|code|" + side + "|" + linkId + "|" + offerHash + "|" + answerHash + "|" + b64url(nonceA) + "|" + b64url(nonceB), and side the literal creator or answerer. The link's creator shows the creator code and the answerer shows the answerer code; each app accepts as typed input only the OTHER side's code, which it computes and never displays. A row gives the five inputs and then, under `creator` and under `answerer`, what THAT side's app does with the codes: `shows` is the six digits on its own screen (the code with its own literal; `inputUtf8` and `digestHex` are the derivation of `shows`), and `accepts` is the only six digits it accepts when typed, which is the other side's `shows`, repeated so that nobody has to work out which is which. A code row has no field called `code`. The two codes differ in every row but the last, code[8]: its nonceB was searched for, the first of the oracle's labelled nonces that gives both sides the same six digits, as about one link in a million has (§6.11 "Equal codes"). In that row `shows` and `accepts` are one value on both sides, and the row has the same fields as every other.

typedCode: the check of typed text (§6.11 "Typed input", "A wrong code is not a verdict", "Equal codes"). `typedInto` is the side whose app the text is typed into; the five inputs are carried in the row itself and are those of one of the code rows (code[0], except in the rows whose `why` begins "The inputs of code[7]", whose two codes start with 0, or "The inputs of code[8]", whose two codes are equal); `typed` is the text as typed; and expect.accepted says whether that app accepts it (and so, on its own correct entry only, sets compared = true). The rule: every ASCII space (U+0020) is removed from `typed`, wherever it stands and however many there are, and what is left must be exactly six ASCII digits (U+0030 to U+0039), equal as text to the OTHER side's code. Nothing else is normalised, so none of these is accepted: the code without its leading zero (it is compared as text, not as a number), a tab, a no-break space or a dash between the digits, a seventh digit, the digits of another script, the empty string, spaces alone, and, where the two codes differ, the code on the app's own screen. Where the two codes are equal nothing special happens: each app accepts that code, and must not refuse it for being equal to its own. A wrong code is not a verdict: the design names no string for it (nothing was verified or refused, and the person may type again), so the expectation is a boolean. `typed` is to be passed on exactly as the JSON string decodes: it holds a tab in one row and characters outside ASCII in three, which this ASCII-only file writes as JSON escapes.

Changed on 2026-11-15: the design gave each side of a link its own code (it first had one code, shown on both screens), and the rows for an enrol link to the public instance were written. (1) code: a row had `inputUtf8`, `digestHex` and `code` at its top level; these three are gone, and the row has `creator` and `answerer` instead, each {inputUtf8, digestHex, shows, accepts}. The side literal is new in every inputUtf8, so every digest and every six digits changed, and each `why` was reworded; the inputs of the first seven rows did not change, and the zero-padding row has another nonceB (both of its codes are below 100000). (2) typedCode is new. (3) creator: on the three ok rows expect.code was a six-digit string and is now {shows, accepts}, this device's two codes: shows is the creator code and accepts the answerer code. The `why` of the row `answer` was reworded; no verdict and no other field of a creator row changed. (4) recipient: the 88 rows that were there are unchanged byte for byte; twelve rows are new, at the end, each with a `baked` input; cardChains has five more chains (public-*), and the four that were there are unchanged. accounts, link, derive, fingerprint, commit, reveal, url and envelopes are unchanged byte for byte.

Changed on 2026-11-15, second batch, with three rules written into the design: §6.11 ("Typed input", "A wrong code is not a verdict", "Equal codes"), §4.4 ("At the baked origin the baked root always comes first") and §2.4 (the depth of a host offer is decided before any general JSON parser sees it). (1) code: one row is new, the last, code[8], whose two codes are equal; the eight rows that were there are unchanged byte for byte. (2) typedCode: twenty rows are new, after the eight that were there, which are unchanged byte for byte. The shape of a row is the same, but two things a reader could rely on before no longer hold: a row's five inputs are not always those of code[0], and `typed` is not always six ASCII digits. (3) recipient: eighteen rows are new, at the end: three very deep host offers (host-json-nest-986, host-json-nest-986-enrol-offer, host-json-nest-1001-no-purpose), thirteen connect, register and setup links to the origin the build bakes (the rows whose names begin connect-public-instance, register-public-instance or setup-public-instance, and order-baked-root-before-the-offer-root) and two links to another origin on a build that bakes (connect-another-origin-on-a-build-that-bakes, setup-another-origin-on-a-build-that-bakes). expect.pinRoot is a new field, present only on the ok rows of a link to the baked origin: on the two new ones (connect-public-instance, register-public-instance) and on two that were there, enrol-public-instance and enrol-public-instance-chain-extends-the-pin, which gained that one field and nothing else. The other 98 recipient rows that were there are unchanged byte for byte, and so are cardChains, creator and every other section.

Changed on 2026-11-15, third batch, with rules written into design §2.4 and §4.4. Every row that was there is unchanged byte for byte, and so are cardChains and every section but recipient and creator. (1) recipient: thirteen rows are new, at the end. An offer envelope above the cap of 2,732 characters is unopenable, refused before any key is derived (offer-envelope-over-the-cap: 2,734 characters, the smallest above the cap, of an envelope that opens under the link's key to the connect offer frame followed by zero bytes, since no offer frame alone makes an envelope that large), and the envelope at the cap is not (offer-envelope-at-the-cap: bad_frame, from the padded frame). kind_mismatch from a host offer's own purpose (enrol-offer-on-a-setup-link), and non_canonical first for a host offer that is not recognised, whatever kind it seems to name (host-json-too-deep-names-the-other-kind, host-json-trailing-comma-names-the-other-kind); kind_mismatch from the form for the two kinds the earlier rows did not use (signed-frame-on-a-setup-link, host-json-on-a-register-link). Under an existing Trust Gate pin at the baked origin (enrol-public-instance-raises-a-trust-gate-pin: ok, pinRoot baked; enrol-public-instance-trust-gate-pin-on-another-card-0: card0_mismatch; order-pin-before-the-baked-root-under-a-trust-gate-pin: fork). A setup link at the baked origin whose chain fails the baked checks on its instanceId (setup-public-instance-id-differs: instance_mismatch). `pin.root` is a new, optional field of a row's pin, present only on the three Trust Gate rows. (2) creator: two rows are new, at the end: answer-envelope-over-the-cap (unopenable) and answer-envelope-at-the-cap (bad_frame), built as the recipient's. (3) An offer or answer of a row may now be longer than 2,732 characters, on those two rows only.

Changed on 2026-11-15, fourth batch, with the dot-atom and domain rule of emailNorm (spec 01 §5.5), which the email_b64n type of an enrol offer uses: two recipient rows are new, at the end, enrol-offer-email-with-an-uppercase-letter and enrol-offer-email-in-a-display-name-form (carol<carol@example.com>: lower case, one @, printable ASCII, refused only by the dot-atom rule), both non_canonical. Every other row is unchanged byte for byte, and every address the file already carried (carol@example.com in the enrol offer, alice@example.com) is its own emailNorm.

url.compose: https://andvaripass.com/l#v2.<O>.<S>.<F>, O = b64url(UTF-8 origin), S = b64url(s), F the creator fingerprint or "-". url.parse: total parsing; expect.verdict ok with the three values, or bad_link. White space (space, tab, CR and LF, and nothing else: a form feed or a vertical tab stays and makes the link malformed) is removed first, wherever it stands; the input is the whole URL or only the fragment, with or without its #; nothing before the # is checked; exactly four parts; O must be canonical base64url of an origin of §2.2; S canonical and 32 bytes; F "-" or canonical and 16 bytes; at most 512 characters once the white space is removed.
envelopes: seal rows are byte-exact (spec 02 §2 envelope, fixed nonce). open rows say whether an envelope opens under a key and AD.

recipient: opening a link (§6.8). Inputs: the link text, `now`, the answer of GET /links/{linkId} (`server.status`, `server.body`), the card chain the origin serves (`cards` names an entry of `cardChains`), this device's pin for that origin (`pin`, or null), the account's contacts (userId -> pinned identity key) and, on the rows that have it, `baked`: what this build bakes, PUBLIC_INSTANCE = {origin, instanceId, card0Hash, kind} (§0.3; spec/public-instance.json holds placeholders until the cut-over, so each such row carries the constants it is graded with). A row without `baked` opens a link to an origin that no build bakes, and reads the same on every build. The first failure is the verdict, in §2.4's order: bad_link; link_unknown (404), link_expired (410), link_used (200, state answered); unopenable (the envelope does not open under offerKey with its AD, or `server.body.offer` is longer than 2,732 characters, which is refused before any key is derived); unknown_format, and kind_mismatch from the form alone; for a signed offer the parse verdicts, kind_mismatch (its own kind), creator_mismatch, signer_not_pinned_key, bad_signature; for host JSON non_canonical unless it is printable JSON with a string purpose (RFC 8259 exactly, with at most 32 containers open at once: the depth is decided on the bytes, or by a parser that stops at the limit, before any general JSON parser sees the text, so the three host-json-nest rows of about a thousand containers are non_canonical and must not overflow a stack), unknown_format for another purpose, kind_mismatch when the purpose names the other host kind (known before the template is parsed; a host offer that is not recognised is non_canonical or unknown_format first, whatever kind it seems to name), the template's parse, and creator_mismatch when F is not "-"; then link_mismatch, origin_mismatch (the offer's origin is not the link's), offer_expired (expiresAt > now must hold), reported_creator_mismatch; then the pinning step. Pinning: if this device holds a pin for the origin, the served chain is compared with it first and anything but ok stops (fork, withheld). Then, for a signed offer, the link-offer root of §2.4's pinning row: withheld for an empty chain, origin_mismatch when the chain's newest card names another origin than the link's, card_not_in_chain, instance_mismatch. For a setup offer: already_set_up when the instance serves any card. For an enrol offer, which is not a root: the typed-address root (withheld, origin_mismatch), after which the Trust Gate shows. At the origin the build bakes (the link's origin is `baked.origin`) the baked root always comes first, whatever the kind of link (§4.4, §6.8 step 5), after the comparison with an existing pin as for every root: withheld for an empty chain, origin_mismatch, card0_mismatch (card 0 does not hash to baked.card0Hash), instance_mismatch (baked.instanceId), in that order. Then the link adds its own check on top: a connect or register link, card_not_in_chain and instance_mismatch (the offer's cardHash must be in the chain under the offer's instanceId); an enrol link, nothing more, and no Trust Gate; a setup link is refused, already_set_up for every served chain that passed the baked checks (an empty one was withheld, so nothing is signed). A link to any other origin gets the same answer whether or not the row has `baked`. On ok, keyChanged says whether the key_changed prompt is due: a known contact with another key. expect.pinRoot stands on the ok rows of a link to the baked origin, and on no other row: it is the root that the pin for that origin records, in the words of passwordgate.json's `root`, and it is `baked` whatever kind of link was opened (a password pin: the build, not the link, vouches for the instance; an enrol link there leaves `baked`, not `enrol`, and a connect or register link `baked`, not `link_offer`). A row's `pin` is {card0Hash, seq, hash} or null, and may also carry `root`, the root that existing pin records, in passwordgate.json's words (baked, kit, setup, trust_gate, link_offer, enrol). `root` is optional: where it is absent the reader gives the pin its own default, as before this field existed. Three rows carry it, all `trust_gate`. It changes no verdict: under an existing pin at the baked origin the pin is compared first, as always, and the baked checks then run on the same chain (§4.4, "Under an existing pin at the baked origin"): when they pass, the pin's root becomes baked whatever it was (expect.pinRoot), and a pinned chain whose card 0 is not the baked one is card0_mismatch. On the one row with pinRoot whose pin has no `root` (enrol-public-instance-chain-extends-the-pin), that pin was itself made through the baked root, as every first pin at the baked origin is on a build that bakes it: a harness gives it the root `baked`, and it stays `baked`. On the rows without pinRoot this file does not state the root.

creator: processing an answer on the creating device (§6.8). Inputs: the device's link records by linkId, `now`, and the served row {linkId, answer, answererUserId}. Order: unknown_link (no record, or now >= the record's expiresAt: expiry is exclusive); unopenable (the envelope does not open, or `served.answer` is longer than 2,732 characters, which is refused before any key is derived); the parse verdicts; signer_not_pinned_key (the signer must map to the answer's own fromKey); bad_signature; link_mismatch; offer_mismatch; misaddressed; reported_answerer_mismatch. On ok, answerHash = H(the answer frame) and `code` holds this device's two codes, named as in the code rows: code.shows is the creator code, which its screen shows, and code.accepts is the answerer code, the only typed input it accepts and one it never displays.

No row, because they are flow rules and not verdicts: a move met while a link is opened under an existing pin (handled as a move first, and the link is opened again afterwards), and an answer of GET /links other than 200, 404 or 410 (a flow stop). No row has a field for the Trust Gate: whether it shows is in each row's `why`, and for a link to the baked origin it never shows.
The extension handles no links and grades none of these rows (§17).

recipient.name: host-json-purpose-is-a-number

recipient.name: host-json-foreign-purpose-with-white-space
recipient.why: The same with white space between its tokens: RFC 8259 allows it, so the object is recognised and its purpose is foreign. (White space matters only to a template's own strict parse.)

recipient.name: host-json-bare-token
recipient.why: A bare token as a value: not RFC 8259. A lenient library parser that reads it would go on to the foreign purpose and answer unknown_format.

recipient.name: host-json-nan
recipient.why: NaN is not a JSON value.

recipient.name: host-json-trailing-comma

recipient.name: host-json-second-object

recipient.name: host-json-key-twice
recipient.why: A key that appears twice at the top level.

recipient.name: host-json-purpose-twice-valid-last
recipient.why: purpose twice, a foreign one first and enrol-offer last: refused whichever value comes last.

recipient.name: host-json-purpose-twice-foreign-last
recipient.why: purpose twice, enrol-offer first and a foreign one last.

recipient.name: host-json-escaped-purpose-key
recipient.why: The key purpose spelled with an escape (\u0070urpose): it is the same key, so this is a JSON object with a string purpose, and that purpose is foreign.

recipient.name: host-json-escaped-purpose-key-twice

recipient.name: host-json-escaped-purpose-key-in-an-enrol-offer
recipient.why: A whole enrol offer whose purpose key is spelled with an escape: it is recognised as an enrol offer, and then the template's re-encode compare refuses it.

recipient.name: host-json-nest-32
recipient.why: Exactly 32 containers open at once (the outer object and 31 arrays inside one another): allowed, so the foreign purpose decides.

recipient.name: host-json-nest-33

recipient.name: host-json-no-purpose

recipient.name: host-json-purpose-null

recipient.name: host-json-leading-space

recipient.name: chain-forks-from-the-pin

recipient.name: chain-extends-the-pin
recipient.why: This device already pins card 0 of the same chain.

recipient.name: no-card-served

Cards are public, so a look-alike address can serve the real instance's genuine chain; a device with no pin refuses.

recipient.name: chain-withheld-below-the-pin
recipient.why: This device pins card 1; the served chain ends at card 0. The chain is compared with the existing pin first and anything but ok stops: withheld. (Without the pin the same chain is card_not_in_chain.)

recipient.why: A setup link opened on an instance that already serves cards.

recipient.name: enrol-no-card-served

recipient.name: enrol-chain-names-another-origin

recipient.name: order-form-kind-before-parse
recipient.why: A signed frame that is not canonical, on a link the server reports as enrol: the form decides before any parse.

recipient.name: order-parse-before-own-kind

recipient.name: order-own-kind-before-creator
recipient.why: eve's register offer on alice's connect link.

recipient.name: order-creator-before-signer
recipient.why: An offer that names eve's key and was signed by carol.

recipient.name: order-signer-before-signature
recipient.why: Signed by eve, with the signature broken as well.

recipient.name: order-signature-before-fields
recipient.why: The helper's checks run before the field checks: another linkId under a broken signature.

recipient.name: order-link-before-origin
recipient.why: Another linkId and another origin.

recipient.name: order-origin-before-expiry
recipient.why: Another origin, and expired.

recipient.name: order-expiry-before-reported-creator
recipient.why: Expired, and the server reports another creator.

recipient.name: order-reported-creator-before-pinning
recipient.why: The server reports another creator, and the chain lacks the offer's card.

recipient.name: order-host-kind-before-the-template-parse
recipient.why: A setup offer that is not canonical (a space after a colon), on a link the server reports as enrol. The purpose is recognised before the template is parsed, so kind_mismatch is known first.

recipient.name: order-host-kind-before-the-template-parse-enrol
recipient.why: The other way round: an enrol offer with "v":3 on a link the server reports as setup.

recipient.name: order-pin-before-the-offer-root
recipient.why: This device pins a card of another chain, and the served chain lacks the offer's card: the comparison with the existing pin comes first, so fork, not card_not_in_chain.

recipient.name: order-origin-before-card-not-in-chain
recipient.why: The served chain names another origin in its newest card, and the offer names a card it does not hold: origin_mismatch comes first.

recipient.name: order-expiry-before-already-set-up
recipient.why: A setup offer past its expiresAt, on an instance that already serves cards: the field checks come before the pinning step.

recipient.name: order-envelope-before-format
recipient.why: An unopenable envelope on a link the server reports as enrol.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance
recipient.why: An enrol link whose origin is the one this build bakes (the public instance): the baked root pins it, in place of the typed-address rule and its Trust Gate. Card 0 of the served chain hashes to the baked card0Hash under the baked instanceId, and the newest card names the baked origin.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-card-0-differs
recipient.why: The baked origin serves a chain whose card 0 names the baked instanceId and origin but does not hash to the baked card0Hash (a new chain after an operator reset, or another server answering for the address). Under the typed-address rule this chain would reach the Trust Gate; the baked root refuses it.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-id-differs
recipient.why: Card 0 hashes to the baked card0Hash, but this build bakes another instanceId: both baked constants must match. (Card 0 carries its instanceId, so only a build whose two constants disagree gets here.)

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-both-differ
recipient.why: The baked origin serves another instance that names that origin as its own: neither card 0's hash nor its instanceId matches. card0_mismatch comes before instance_mismatch in the pinning order.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-no-card-served
recipient.why: The baked origin serves no card: a baked root against an empty chain is withheld.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-serves-another-chain
recipient.why: The baked origin serves another instance's genuine chain, whose cards name that instance's own origin. origin_mismatch comes first, before card0_mismatch and instance_mismatch, which this chain would fail too.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-newest-card-names-another-origin
recipient.why: The public instance's own chain (card 0 matches both baked constants), with a newest card that names another origin than the baked one this device dialed. A first pin never follows a card to another address.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-chain-extends-the-pin
recipient.why: This device already pins card 0 of the public instance's chain: the served chain extends the pin, and the baked root holds.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-withheld-below-the-pin
recipient.why: This device pins card 1 of the public instance's chain; the baked origin serves card 0 only. The chain is compared with the existing pin first and anything but ok stops: withheld. (Without the pin the baked root passes this chain.)

recipient.name: order-pin-before-the-baked-root
recipient.why: This device pins card 1 of the public instance's chain, and the baked origin serves another card 0: the comparison with the existing pin comes first, so fork, not card0_mismatch.

recipient.name: order-expiry-before-the-baked-root
recipient.why: An enrol offer past its expiresAt, on a baked origin that serves another card 0: the field checks come before the pinning step.

recipient.name: enrol-another-origin-on-a-build-that-bakes
recipient.why: The link and chain of the row `enrol`, opened by a build that bakes the public instance. The link's origin is not the baked one, so the baked root has no say: the typed-address rule, then the Trust Gate. (The served card 0 is not the baked one, and need not be.)

recipient.name: host-json-nest-986
recipient.why: The text of host-json-nest-32 and host-json-nest-33 with 986 containers open at once (the outer object and 985 arrays inside one another): as deep as that text can go in an offer, whose envelope is then exactly 2,048 bytes, 2,731 of the 2,732 characters allowed. It is refused for its depth, on the bytes or by a parser that stops at the limit, before any general JSON parser sees it: a parser that recurses once per level can be made to overflow its stack by this text, and that is a crash, not a verdict. (A parser that read all of it would find a purpose the client does not recognise and answer unknown_format.)

recipient.name: host-json-nest-986-enrol-offer
recipient.why: The same depth behind a purpose the client recognises: {"v":2,"purpose":"enrol-offer","x": and then 985 arrays inside one another, on a link the server reports as enrol. Still non_canonical: a recognisable purpose at the front does not carry a text past the depth limit, and no look-ahead for the purpose may hand this text to a general JSON parser either.

recipient.name: host-json-nest-1001-no-purpose
recipient.why: A thousand open brackets: {"x": and then 1,000 arrays inside one another, so 1,001 containers open at once, and no purpose anywhere. non_canonical, for the depth alone and before anything looks for a purpose. With a key this short the envelope holds exactly a thousand arrays.

recipient.name: connect-public-instance
recipient.why: A connect link whose origin is the one this build bakes (the public instance). The baked root comes first, whatever started the connection: card 0 of the served chain hashes to the baked card0Hash under the baked instanceId, and the newest card names the baked origin. Then the link adds its own check on top: the chain holds the offer's cardHash under the offer's instanceId. The pin records root baked (expect.pinRoot), not link_offer: the build, not the link, vouches for the instance. No Trust Gate is shown.

recipient.name: connect-public-instance-card-0-differs
recipient.why: The baked origin serves a chain whose card 0 does not hash to the baked card0Hash (a new chain after an operator reset, or another server answering for the address), and the link was made against that chain: the offer's cardHash is in it, under the offer's instanceId, so the link's own check would pass, and on a build that bakes nothing this link opens. The baked checks run first and refuse it.

recipient.name: connect-public-instance-id-differs
recipient.why: Card 0 hashes to the baked card0Hash, but this build bakes another instanceId: instance_mismatch, from the baked root. The offer names the chain's own instanceId and a card of the chain, so the link's own check would pass. (Card 0 carries its instanceId, so only a build whose two constants disagree gets here.)

recipient.name: connect-public-instance-card-not-in-chain
recipient.why: The baked checks pass (the public instance's own card 0, under the baked instanceId, naming the baked origin), and the served chain does not hold the offer's cardHash (it ends one card earlier): the link's own check, on top of the baked root.

recipient.name: connect-public-instance-offer-names-another-instance
recipient.why: The baked checks pass, and the offer's cardHash is in the served chain under another instanceId than the offer names: instance_mismatch, this time from the link's own check (the baked instanceId is the chain's).

recipient.name: connect-public-instance-no-card-served
recipient.why: The baked origin serves no card: an empty chain is withheld under the baked root, as under every root.

recipient.name: order-baked-root-before-the-offer-root
recipient.why: Two things wrong at once at the baked origin: card 0 does not hash to the baked card0Hash, and the served chain does not hold the offer's cardHash. The baked checks run first, so card0_mismatch; card_not_in_chain is what a build that bakes nothing answers.

recipient.name: register-public-instance
recipient.why: A register link to the baked origin: the same order, kind register. The baked root first, then the offer's cardHash under the offer's instanceId; the pin's root is baked, and no Trust Gate is shown.

recipient.name: register-public-instance-card-0-differs
recipient.why: A register link made against another card 0 at the baked origin: its own check would pass (the offer's cardHash is in the served chain under the offer's instanceId), and the baked checks, which run first, refuse it.

recipient.name: register-public-instance-card-not-in-chain
recipient.why: A register link to the baked origin whose cardHash the served chain does not hold (it ends one card earlier): the baked checks pass, then the link's own check.

recipient.name: setup-public-instance-no-card-served
recipient.why: A setup link whose origin is the one this build bakes, and that origin serves no card. At any other origin this is how a setup link opens (the row `setup`). Here the baked root comes first and an empty chain is withheld under it, so nothing is signed: a build that bakes an instance never signs that instance's card 0.

recipient.name: setup-public-instance-already-set-up
recipient.why: The baked origin serves the public instance's own chain, which passes the baked checks: a setup link is refused there, already_set_up.

recipient.name: setup-public-instance-card-0-differs
recipient.why: The baked origin serves another card 0. The baked checks run first, so card0_mismatch; already_set_up is what a build that bakes nothing answers.

recipient.name: connect-another-origin-on-a-build-that-bakes
recipient.why: The link and chain of the row `connect`, opened by a build that bakes the public instance. The link's origin is not the baked one, so what the build bakes has no say: the answer of `connect`, field for field, through the link-offer root, and no pinRoot.

recipient.name: setup-another-origin-on-a-build-that-bakes
recipient.why: The link of the row `setup`, opened by a build that bakes the public instance: its origin is not the baked one and serves no card, so the setup link opens as it does on every build.

recipient.name: offer-envelope-over-the-cap
recipient.why: The offer envelope is 2,734 characters (2,050 bytes), above the cap of 2,732 characters (§6.6): unopenable, refused before any key is derived. It is otherwise a good envelope: sealed under this link's offerKey with its AD, it opens, to alice's connect offer frame (that of `link`) followed by 1,413 zero bytes. No offer frame alone can make an envelope this large (a frame is at most 1,125 bytes), so the padding is inside the seal. An engine that skipped the cap would open it and answer bad_frame, as the row offer-envelope-at-the-cap does. (2,733 characters is not a length unpadded base64url can have, so 2,734 is the smallest envelope above the cap.)

recipient.name: offer-envelope-at-the-cap
recipient.why: The same construction one byte smaller: 2,049 bytes, exactly 2,732 characters, which the cap allows (an envelope is refused only when it is LARGER than 2,732 characters). It opens, to alice's connect offer frame followed by 1,412 zero bytes: a signed frame of 2,007 bytes, longer than 1,125, so bad_frame.

recipient.name: enrol-offer-on-a-setup-link
recipient.why: A well-formed enrol offer (the one of the row `enrol`) on a link the server reports as setup: its purpose is recognised, and it names the other host kind, so kind_mismatch, before the template is parsed. (The row setup-offer-on-an-enrol-link is the other way round.)

recipient.name: host-json-too-deep-names-the-other-kind
recipient.why: The setup offer of the row `setup` with one more key, "x", holding 32 arrays one inside another: 33 containers open at once, on a link the server reports as enrol. Too deep, so it is not recognised, and a host offer that is not recognised is non_canonical first, whatever kind it seems to name. A reader that recognised it anyway would find a setup offer and answer kind_mismatch.

recipient.name: host-json-trailing-comma-names-the-other-kind
recipient.why: The enrol offer of the row `enrol` with a comma before its closing brace, on a link the server reports as setup. Not RFC 8259, so it is not recognised: non_canonical comes first, whatever kind it seems to name. A lenient parser that skipped the comma would recognise an enrol offer and answer kind_mismatch.

recipient.name: signed-frame-on-a-setup-link
recipient.why: kind_mismatch from the form alone: the server reports kind setup, and the envelope opens to a signed frame (alice's connect offer). (signed-frame-on-a-host-link is the same on an enrol link.)

recipient.name: host-json-on-a-register-link
recipient.why: kind_mismatch from the form alone: the server reports kind register, and the envelope opens to host JSON (the enrol offer of the row `enrol`). (host-json-on-a-connect-link is the same on a connect link.)

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-raises-a-trust-gate-pin
recipient.why: This device already pins the baked origin through the Trust Gate (pin.root trust_gate, made on card 0 of the public instance's own chain, for example by a build that did not bake it). The served chain extends the pin, and the baked checks then pass on the same chain: the pin's root becomes baked (expect.pinRoot), raised from trust_gate. No Trust Gate is shown.

recipient.name: enrol-public-instance-trust-gate-pin-on-another-card-0
recipient.why: This device pins the baked origin through the Trust Gate, on a chain whose card 0 is not the baked one, and the served chain is that chain, so it extends the pin. The pin comparison passes; the baked checks then run on the same chain and refuse it: card0_mismatch, and the device does not use that instance until the person forgets the server.

recipient.name: order-pin-before-the-baked-root-under-a-trust-gate-pin
recipient.why: The same Trust Gate pin on another card 0, and the baked origin now serves the public instance's own chain, which forks from the pin (its card 0 differs). The pin comparison comes first: fork, although that chain would pass the baked checks.

recipient.name: setup-public-instance-id-differs
recipient.why: A setup link to the baked origin, which serves the public instance's own chain: card 0 hashes to the baked card0Hash, but this build bakes another instanceId, so the chain fails the baked checks with instance_mismatch, not already_set_up. (Card 0 carries its instanceId, so only a build whose two constants disagree gets here.)

recipient.name: enrol-offer-email-with-an-uppercase-letter
recipient.why: The enrol offer of the row `enrol` with its email the base64url of Carol@example.com: email_b64n must already be its own emailNorm, so an upper-case letter is non_canonical (spec 01 §5.1).

recipient.name: enrol-offer-email-in-a-display-name-form
recipient.why: The enrol offer of the row `enrol` with its email the base64url of carol<carol@example.com>: lower case, one @, every byte printable ASCII, but the local part is not a dot-atom, so the address has no emailNorm and email_b64n refuses it (spec 01 §5.5).

creator.name: record-one-millisecond-before-expiry

creator.name: answer-signature-flipped

creator.name: order-signer-before-signature
